title: What is known about 1RB0LA_0RC0LE_0RD1RC_1LD1RE_1LA1RF_---0RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LA_0RC0LE_0RD1RC_1LD1RE_1LA1RF_---0RB.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project; an outside Rocq proof has since shown that it never halts when started on a blank tape. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it never halts. Busycoq pull request 107 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-19) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. Lean proves both passes over the bulk of the tape (kernel) and no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in 109 steps. On their own these leave the question open.

What it does. Seen at the right end, the tape is a list of blocks (110)n separated by short separators (10, 1, 0 1). The leftward pass rewrites every 110 as 010 (seen from the left end the tape is blocks of (100)n), and the rightward pass turns them back. On each round trip the last block grows by two and the first few blocks are rewritten like the low digits of a counter; now and then the change runs further right, like a carry.
Where a halt would come from. Only F reading a 0 halts, i.e. E standing on 1 0 (halt_E). In the run F always reads a 1, and the proof shows that this never changes.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,366 cells have been visited and 20,923 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.90·10<sup>11</sup> steps (accelerated run, blocks of 6)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/c/rleaccel.cpp (blocks of 6 cells, runs of a block crossed in one step, and cycle jumps, each used only after its one-cycle rule has been proved symbolically for all lengths above the minimums it needs; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 39,200,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt, in 10 seconds. That is more than 1.90·1011 machine steps. It found no rule that repeats forever, so it does not decide the machine.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.47). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.472).

claims.title: Every way to a halt
claims.text: Two steps before any halt the machine is in 1 B>1 or D>1 1 0; no other configuration halts within three steps.

claims.title: The two passes
claims.text: Moving right, C turns each 010 into 101, seven steps a word: 1 (010)n becomes (110)n 1. Moving left, A turns each 011 back into 010, fifteen steps a word. Both for any n.

claims.title: The halting situation
claims.text: E>1 0 halts on the next step; F is entered only from E reading a 1.

claims.title: The list of blocks
claims.text: At the right-end turns of the first 4·104 steps the tape is a list of 110-blocks with short separators; the last block has 4, 6, 8, 10, … copies on consecutive trips (steps 561, 756, 1,089, 1,456), and only the first few blocks change on most trips.

claims.title: New last blocks, and how deep a round trip reaches
claims.text: The last run of 110 grows by two copies a round trip until a carry reaches it. Then it is frozen and a new last run starts: at steps 1,909, 13,265, 47,957, 319,522 and 98,472,504, with frozen runs of 11, 23, 35, 133 and 3923 copies. No new run starts between 9.8·107 and 3·1010 steps, while the last run grows past 50,000 copies. Of the 4,170 round trips in the first 108 steps, more than 90% change the list of runs at 19 or more runs from the front.

claims.title: Size of the tape description (family screen)
claims.text: At the 8 records between 2.6·10<sup>8</sup> and 1.6·10<sup>10</sup> steps (first new leftmost or rightmost cell after each threshold 10<sup>6</sup>·4^k) the tape has 18,358 to 157,898 visited cells and compresses to 41 to 71 level-2 tokens (repeats of a word of at most 40 cells, then repeats of groups of such tokens).

claims.title: Proposed family: F06, block-list counters
claims.text: The description grows slowly if at all: 41 to 71 level-2 tokens at the records from 2.6·10<sup>8</sup> to 1.6·10<sup>10</sup> steps, and 27 to 63 runs in the macro simulator (blocks of 3 cells) at the sampled records from 10<sup>6</sup> to 2·10<sup>12</sup> steps. The frozen run of 3,923 copies made near step 10<sup>8</sup> is still there at 1.6·10<sup>10</sup> steps, the last run has 48,470 copies, and the short blocks to their left differ from record to record. A list of blocks whose front is rewritten like the low digits of a counter, with carries that reach further at longer and longer intervals (new last runs at steps 1,909, 13,265, 47,957, 319,522 and 98,472,504), is the shape of F06.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape? (this repository’s own ledger)
claims.text: Not decided by the results on this page alone. It is decided outside: busycoq pull request 107 proves that it never halts (see the verdict).

explainer.lede: It never halts. The tape is a list of blocks of 110, and the head makes round trips across all of it: each trip adds two copies of 110 to the block at the right end and rewrites a short counter at the far left end. The proof finds a tape shape that comes back, a little bigger, after exactly 137,438,953,469 round trips, and so comes back for ever.

facts.text: No halt in the run-length accelerator (proved cycle jumps, blocks of 6).
No halt in the C simulator; 36,366 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A counter that comes back after 137,438,953,469 round trips
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 107 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1, and it uses no axioms.

The shape of the tape. Write (110)n for the word 110 written n times. The proof watches the machine when the head is at the right end of the tape, in state C, with only 0s to its right. Reading leftward from the head, the tape is then: a long block (110)t+2; a frozen middle part, made of runs of 110 of fixed lengths (about 11.7 million, then 386,565, 3,884 and 66 copies, with short pieces between them) that never change again; then (110)2 10 (110)m+2; and at the far left a fixed pattern of about a hundred short blocks that works as a counter. Call this configuration Inv(t, m). It is the same shape for every pair of numbers t and m.

The repeated step. One round trip takes the head from the right end to the far left and back. Moving through a block of 110 the head rewrites each copy and later restores it, so blocks that the trip only crosses come back unchanged, whatever their length; the proof shows this once for all lengths (tailBounces_frame_atoms). Every round trip adds two copies of 110 to the block next to the head, and changes the counter at the far left. The main theorem is that after exactly 237 − 3 = 137,438,953,469 round trips the counter is back where it started, except that m has grown by one: Inv(t, m) leads to Inv(t + 274,877,906,938, m + 1).

Why it never halts. This holds for every t and m, so the step can be applied again and again, and each application takes at least one machine step. The machine therefore runs for ever once it reaches Inv(t, m) for some t and m. From a blank tape it reaches Inv(1,549,833,076,750, 0) after 51 accelerated operations and one more cycle.

What is proved and what is computed. The far-left counter goes through about 137 billion round trips per cycle, far too many to run one by one. The proof builds them from small pieces: 2,579 basic rules, each one round trip on a short pattern, are checked by running the machine (130,137 small steps in all), and 1,334 larger rules are each made from two or more smaller ones, like the digits of a binary counter. The two largest, of 236 − 4 and 236 − 7 round trips, make up all but eight round trips of a cycle. The computer checks every rule with Coq’s vm_compute; the soundness of combining rules and of ignoring the passive blocks, and the cycle theorem for every m, are proved by induction.

sections.heading: A list of 110-blocks
html: Stop the simulator at each turn of the head at the right end and write b for 110 and c for 10. The tape is a list of runs of b separated by short pieces:

561  c c 1 b2 0 1 b c b4 1 1 D>0
  756  c c 1 b 1 b2 c b6 1 1 D>0
1,089  c c 1 1 b c b c c b8 1 1 D>0
1,456  c c 1 b2 0 b2 1 b10 1 1 D>0

The last run grows by two on every round trip; the runs in front of it are rewritten a little each time, like the low digits of a counter, and occasionally the rewriting reaches further to the right like a carry. That is why the right edge grows like the square root of the step count: one more pair of words per trip, each trip as long as the tape.

Both passes are slow zig-zags. Moving right, C rewrites each 010 as 101 in seven steps, so 1 (010)n becomes (110)n 1; moving left, A rewrites each 011 as 010 in fifteen steps. Lean proves both for every n (pass_right, pass_left).

The machine halts only if E stands on 1 0 (halt_E). This repository did not pin down the exact effect of one round trip on the list; the proof above does it for a whole cycle of round trips and shows that the halting situation never arises.

sections.heading: Which family it belongs to
html: The 22 machines of family F09 (“bouncers over lists of counters, not yet classified”) were screened in one way. The machine runs from blank tape for 2·1010 steps; each time the tape reaches a new cell after a threshold, the tape is compressed twice: first repeats of one word, then repeats of groups of words. If the tape is a few growing blocks and a bounded rest, the number of level-2 tokens stays bounded while the tape grows. Everything in this section is observed in one run. None of it is proved.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.47). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.472).
After 109 steps the tape spans 36,366 cells (4,399 left of the start, 21,934 right), with a density of 1s of 0.575.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is described in the proof section.

family: two-sided bouncer, list of 110-blocks with a counter at the left end
summary: Round trips over a tape of 110-blocks separated by short separators; the last block grows by two per trip while the blocks near the left end change like the digits of a counter. Open. Accelerated run: no halt in 1.90e11 steps. Decided outside: busycoq PR 107 proves in Rocq that it never halts (compiled here).
